analysis.one_liner: Requires retail stores to accept cash for in-person purchases and bans cash surcharges.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action in the Senate before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require retail businesses that take in-person payments at physical locations to accept cash for sales under $2,000, and it would forbid them from charging cash customers a higher price than card customers. It was introduced with one Republican cosponsor and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: People without credit or debit cards: the roughly 1 in 20 US households without bank accounts, the underbanked, elderly customers, and people who prefer cash for budgeting or privacy. Any consumer who has been turned away at a cashless store gains a legal right to pay cash.

how_it_helps.text: Requires retail businesses accepting in-person payments at a physical location to accept cash for sales under $2,000 and prohibits charging cash customers a higher price than non-cash customers [S2][S3].

Lets consumers enforce the right in court, with civil penalties of up to $2,500 for a first violation and $5,000 for repeat violations, and permits the Attorney General to intervene in actions of general public importance [S3].

Protects state, local, and tribal laws that are stronger than the federal rule, and directs regulators to report annually on the geographic distribution of ATMs, a step toward understanding where cash access is scarce [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Cashless retailers and restaurants, which would bear the cost of handling, counting, and safeguarding cash and lose the convenience of card-only checkout. Card networks and payment processors would also lose some transaction volume, since interchange fees are charged on electronic payments but not on cash.

drawbacks.text: Handling cash is not free: businesses must count drawers, make bank deposits, and face theft risk, which is a real cost for small shops and chains alike, and an honest supporter of the bill acknowledges this trade-off.

The bill gives businesses escape hatches that could blunt the mandate: they need not accept $50 bills or larger for five years, and they can avoid the cash requirement by offering a no-fee on-site card-conversion machine [S3].
Civil penalties are modest (up to $2,500 first offense), so enforcement would likely depend on individual lawsuits rather than routine compliance checks [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers without cards, the benefit is direct: cash stays legal tender in practice, not just in name, at every store that serves walk-in customers. For everyone else the effect is small. The main costs fall on retailers through cash handling and security, which are real but generally modest for a business already equipped to take cash. On balance a narrow, low-cost protection aimed at people the card economy tends to leave out.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee in June 2022, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Robert Menendez introduced the Payment Choice Act of 2022 on June 23, 2022, joined by Sen. Kevin Cramer as its sole cosponsor [S1][S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on the day it was introduced [S1][S5].
The action history shows no further activity: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that refuse cash and the payment processors behind card transactions are better off: they can continue card-only checkout with no federal penalty, and the millions of unbanked Americans still have no federal right to pay cash. Two subsequent Congresses reintroduced similar versions, so the idea is not gone, but as of the 117th Congress nothing happened.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Cashless retailers and card payment processors

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.role: US Senator from New Jersey, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought Senate Banking Committee action.

for.name: Sen. Kevin Cramer
for.role: US Senator from North Dakota, sole cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under Chairman Sherrod Brown (D-OH)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Payment card networks and cashless-payment vendors
against.role: Card issuers and processors whose fee revenue depends on electronic transactions
against.what_they_did: Have publicly opposed cash mandates through industry groups, arguing card-only operation is safer and cheaper for merchants.

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat sponsored the bill and its only cosponsor was a Republican; no party bloc ever voted on it, so its floor support was never tested.

industries.note: Cash mandates cut into card transaction volume, and processors earn interchange fees on electronic payments but nothing on cash. Their interest in staying card-only runs against consumers who need a cash option.

industries.industry: Retail chains, restaurants, and other cashless-adopting merchants
industries.note: The bill forces stores that accept in-person payments to take cash under $2,000, adding cash handling, deposit, and security costs. Some retailers adopted cashless checkout to cut those costs, so the mandate reverses part of that saving.

industries.industry: Cash-in-transit and cash-handling services (armored carriers, cash recyclers)
industries.note: A guaranteed cash economy keeps demand alive for businesses that transport, count, and secure cash for retailers. That is a narrow commercial benefit, not a consumer one.
